rubric: DISCRETE MATHEMATICS / COUNTING AND LOGIC / CHAPTER 3

slides.title: Combinatorics: permutations and combinations
slides.main: Two rules and three counters hold up almost all engineering estimates.

captions: Combinatorics: permutations and combinations
An estimate like "this brute force will finish in a hundred years" starts with the ability to count the options
Combinatorics is the arithmetic of choice: the number of ways is built from small decisions
Two rules and three counters — almost all engineering estimates rest on them

body.text: Every estimate of the kind "this brute force will finish in a hundred years" and every hack-resistant password starts with the ability to count the options without listing them.

slides.title: The sum rule
slides.sub: Exactly one choice from non-overlapping groups
slides.main: The number of execution paths is added up across the branches — like the options in a menu.

captions: The sum rule: we choose exactly one thing, the groups do not overlap
Three options in the first group and four in the second — seven in all
Three soups or four salads — seven ways to choose a first course
In code this is branching: the number of execution paths is added up across the branches

body.text: In code this is branching: each branch of a condition is its own group of options, and the total number of execution paths is added up across the branches.

slides.title: The product rule
slides.sub: Several independent choices in a row
slides.main: As soon as you see a chain of independent choices — multiply.

captions: The product rule is noticeably more powerful than the sum rule
Several independent choices in a row: the number of options multiplies — 2 · 3 = 6
A four-digit PIN code: ten possibilities at each position — 10⁴ = 10 000
Nested loops are a direct embodiment of the rule: the body runs length × length times
As soon as you see a chain of independent choices — multiply

body.text: Nested loops are a direct embodiment of the product rule: the outer loop over one list, the inner over another, and the number of iterations of the body is the product of the lengths.

slides.title: The password space
slides.sub: Length multiplies, the alphabet raises the base
slides.main: A brute-forcer is limited not by the attacker's talent but by the size of the space of options.

captions: Let's apply the product rule to passwords
Eight characters out of ninety-five — 95⁸, about 6.6 quadrillion options
Each extra character multiplies the space by 95 — very fast growth
A long password of plain words is usually stronger than a short one of "clever" symbols
Brute force is limited not by the attacker's talent but by the size of the space

frames.text: about six and a half quadrillion
bar length — the order of magnitude of the number of options
each character of length — ×95 to the time

body.text: A simple security conclusion: the space grows faster with length than with any special characters in a short password.

slides.title: Factorial
slides.sub: The product of all numbers from one to n
slides.main: The factorial overtakes the exponential already at modest numbers — and no hardware will save you.

captions: To count orderings we need our own unit — the factorial
n! is the product of all numbers from 1 to n: 4! = 4 · 3 · 2 · 1 = 24
It grows frighteningly: 10! is more than three and a half million, 20! is past a quintillion
n! catches up with and overtakes the exponential at modest numbers — and hardware won't help

frames.text: n = 1 … 15, vertical axis — order of magnitude (logarithm)

body.text: This is exactly why problems of brute-forcing all orderings so quickly become impossible.

slides.title: Permutations
slides.sub: Arrange n objects in places — n! ways
slides.main: A full enumeration of all orderings runs into the factorial: for large n approximate algorithms are needed.

captions: A permutation is a way to arrange n objects in places; there are exactly n! ways
Ten talks at a conference — 10! schedule options, more than 3.5 million
The traveling salesman: visit all cities by the shortest route — as many options as permutations
With 50 cities the full brute force never finishes — hence approximate algorithms

frames.text: routes — impossible to enumerate in a reasonable time

body.text: That is exactly why approximate algorithms are invented for such problems instead of an honest brute force.

slides.title: Arrangements
slides.sub: Choosing k from n when order matters
slides.main: If swapping two chosen items gives a different combination — count an arrangement.

captions: Now we choose not everything but a part — and see whether order matters
Gold, silver, bronze among twenty: three different awards, 20 · 19 · 18 = 6 840 ways
The formula in words: divide n! by (n − k)! — cut off the tail of those left without a place
A PIN code without repeated digits: 10 · 9 · 8 · 7 = 10!/6! = 5 040 options
If swapping two chosen items gives a different combination — we count an arrangement

frames.text: digits do not repeat: the choice narrows

slides.title: Combinations
slides.sub: Order doesn't matter — divide by k!
slides.main: C(n, k) is the most widely used number in applied combinatorics.

captions: If order doesn't matter, we count combinations: six orderings of one trio are indistinguishable
A combination is an arrangement divided by k!: we divide by all the permutations inside the group
Five cards from fifty-two — C(52, 5), about 2.6 million hands
Two reviewers from six — C(6, 2) = 15 options
A selection with and without order differs by exactly a factor of k!

body.text: The same selection with and without regard to order differs by a factor of k!.

slides.title: Poker categories
slides.main: First count all outcomes, then group by the property: the rarity of a category makes it higher.

captions: The poker numbers show how combinations compress the space of outcomes
There are two and a half million hands, but only about ten ranking categories
Millions of hands spread across the categories very unevenly — rarity makes a category higher
A general technique: count all outcomes, group by the property, count the group
The ratio of the group size to the whole is the probability: four of a kind is about 0.024 %

frames.text: the share of the group in the whole is the probability

body.text: This ratio is already a probability, but let's not get ahead of ourselves today.

slides.title: The number of pairs: C(n, 2)
slides.main: C(n, 2) lives everywhere you need to compare all pairs without repeats and mirror duplicates.

captions: A special case of combinations is the number of pairs: C(n, 2) = n(n − 1) / 2
Ten people will shake hands C(10, 2) = 45 times
In code: the second index is always greater than the first — all pairs without repeats and mirror duplicates
This is also the number of edges of a complete graph: 100 servers need 4 950 channels

body.text: In code this is the number of iterations of a loop in which the second index is always greater than the first.

slides.title: Checking on small numbers
slides.main: Take a tiny example and count by hand — then the formula can be trusted on large numbers.

captions: The newcomer's main mistake is double counting: order taken into account where there is none
The cure: take a tiny example — three friends, choose two
By hand you get three pairs, and C(3, 2) = 3 — the formulas match
Before counting, classify the problem — half of the solution is already ready

slides.title: Linking the chapters
slides.sub: Combinatorics grew out of the past
slides.main: Every new tool reuses the old ones — that is the strength of discrete mathematics.

captions: Notice how the chapters link up
A combination is a subset of size k from a set of size n: combinatorics grew out of sets
The product rule is the Cartesian product from the second chapter, counted by the number of elements
Permutations and combinations will meet us again in the next chapter: Pascal's triangle will be built from them
Every new tool reuses the old ones — that is the value of discrete mathematics

frames.text: each step rests on the previous ones

body.text: Discrete mathematics is valuable precisely for these links.

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: Apply the counters to passwords, PIN codes and poker hands — and estimate brute force before you run it.

captions: Summing up the chapter
Two rules — the sum for mutually exclusive groups and the product for independent choices
Counters: n! for permutations, arrangements with order, C(n, k) without order, C(n, 2) for pairs
Apply them to passwords, PIN codes, poker hands and handshakes — estimate brute force before running it
Next — Pascal's triangle, the binomial theorem and the pigeonhole principle

body.text: The next chapter is Pascal's triangle, the binomial theorem and the pigeonhole principle: three tools that will teach you to see structure where before there was only crude arithmetic.
